title: Lipid Preanalytics: Fasting, Timing, Serum vs Plasma and the Standing Plasma Test
summary: Learn when a lipid profile needs a fasting sample, which collection and patient factors shift lipid results, why lipids dip after a heart attack, why serum runs about 3% above plasma, and how to read the overnight standing plasma test.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 18 Hits 13 (standing plasma test) and 14 (preanalytic rules) and Exam Traps 4 (lipids after a heart attack) and 5 (plasma vs serum). Checked against the EAS/EFLM fasting consensus (Nordestgaard 2016), the PSLD/PoLA laboratory guidelines (Solnica 2024 and 2020), Berberich 2022 and Brahm 2013. Hit 14’s 12-hour fast for TG/LDL-C is superseded by routine nonfasting profiles (register flag rv-lipid-fasting-not-routine). Trap 4’s “wait at least 8 weeks” is qualified: Berberich 2022 reports a post-ACS dip persisting up to 2 months but says peri-ACS values are still informative (register flag rv-post-acs-lipids-informative). Pending (no open source read): the 8-week wait after trauma/infection, 3–4 months postpartum, tourniquet <1–2 min, seated 5 min, chylomicron clearance in 6–9 h, and “EDTA preferred because it stabilizes the sample”. The NCBI Bookshelf Endotext chapter on infection and lipids returned a reCAPTCHA page and was not read.

objectives: State when a fasting lipid sample is worth considering under current consensus.
Name collection, tube and patient factors that shift lipid results, including the post-ACS dip.
Interpret the overnight standing plasma test.

scenes.title: Three lipid tubes, three surprises
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three lipid specimens puzzle the bench — (1) a fasting plasma tube left in the refrigerator overnight shows a creamy layer on top over clear plasma; (2) a patient seen 3 weeks after a heart attack has a reassuringly low LDL-C; (3) an EDTA plasma total cholesterol reads about 3% below a serum result drawn the same morning. Question token: “Disease, timing, or tube?”

cues.text: An invented morning with three lipid puzzles. A fasting plasma tube, left in the refrigerator overnight, has a creamy layer floating on clear plasma.
A patient three weeks after a heart attack has a reassuringly low LDL cholesterol. And a plasma cholesterol reads about three percent below the serum result from the same morning.
Is each one disease, timing, or the tube?

scenes.title: Fasting is no longer the default
scenes.altText: Card 1 (EAS/EFLM 2016 consensus): routine lipid profiles can be nonfasting. Maximal mean changes 1–6 h after habitual meals: triglycerides +26 mg/dL; total cholesterol and LDL-C −8 mg/dL; HDL-C, apoA1, apoB and Lp(a) unchanged. Card 2: when fasting may be considered — nonfasting triglycerides >440 mg/dL (5 mmol/L) in EAS/EFLM 2016, or >400 mg/dL in the PSLD/PoLA 2024 guideline and Berberich 2022; before starting drugs that can cause severe hypertriglyceridaemia; following recovery from hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis.

cues.text: Lipid testing used to start with an overnight fast. The 2016 European consensus on fasting and laboratory reporting now recommends nonfasting lipid profiles for routine use.

A usual meal changes the averages only a little: triglycerides rise about twenty-six milligrams per decilitre, total and LDL cholesterol fall about eight. HDL cholesterol, apolipoproteins A1 and B, and lipoprotein little a do not change.

Fasting still has a place. The consensus says it may be considered when nonfasting triglycerides exceed four hundred and forty milligrams per decilitre; the Polish laboratory guideline and a 2022 review use four hundred.
Fasting samples also help before starting drugs that can cause severe hypertriglyceridaemia, and when following recovery from hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis.

scenes.title: What shifts the numbers
scenes.altText: Card 1 (collection): a tourniquet kept on ≥3 min, or standing >30 min before sampling, can raise cholesterol and triglycerides 10–12% by haemoconcentration; serum TC, HDL-C, LDL-C and TG run about 3% higher than plasma. Card 2 (the patient): intra-individual variability about 5–10% for TC and >20% for TG; third-trimester pregnancy raises TG up to 250%; TC and LDL-C may be lower for several weeks after a cardiovascular event and in chronic inflammation. Token: after an acute coronary syndrome, lower LDL-C and HDL-C and higher TG are seen from 24–96 h, persisting up to 2 months — yet peri-event values are still informative.

cues.text: Some shifts come from collection. A tourniquet left on three minutes or more, or standing over thirty minutes before the draw, concentrates the blood and can raise cholesterol and triglycerides by ten to twelve percent.
The tube matters too: serum lipid results run about three percent higher than plasma. That is an expected matrix difference, not an error.

Some shifts come from the patient. Total cholesterol varies about five to ten percent from day to day and triglycerides more than twenty. Late pregnancy can raise triglycerides by up to two hundred and fifty percent.

After an acute coronary syndrome, LDL and HDL cholesterol fall and triglycerides rise from about one to four days, and this can persist for up to two months. Even so, values from that period are still informative for treatment.

scenes.title: Reading the standing plasma test
scenes.altText: Schematic tubes after overnight refrigerated standing. Tube A: creamy supernatant over a clear infranatant = chylomicrons persisting after a 12–14 h fast (familial chylomicronaemia, HLP type 1). Tube B: creamy supernatant over a turbid infranatant = chylomicrons plus excess VLDL (mixed hyperlipidaemia, HLP type 5). Tube C: turbid without a cream layer at the higher end of simple hypertriglyceridaemia = large VLDL (HLP type 4). Hook answers: (1) fasting chylomicronaemia — check secondary causes and a repeat profile; (2) a post-heart-attack dip — the value is still informative, do not read it as low risk; (3) the expected serum–plasma difference.

cues.text: The standing plasma test: leave plasma in the refrigerator overnight. Chylomicrons are light and float. A creamy top layer over clear plasma means chylomicrons persisting after a twelve to fourteen hour fast, as in familial chylomicronaemia, type 1.

A creamy top over cloudy plasma means chylomicrons plus excess VLDL, as in mixed hyperlipidaemia, type 5. Cloudy plasma with no cream layer can come from large VLDL in simple hypertriglyceridaemia, type 4.
Back to the hook. Tube one is fasting chylomicronaemia. Tube two is the dip after a heart attack: do not read it as low risk, and the value can still guide treatment.
Tube three is the expected difference: serum runs about three percent above plasma.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Every lipid panel needs a 12-hour fast” (✓ nonfasting is routine; consider fasting when nonfasting TG >440 or >400 mg/dL); “Low LDL-C weeks after a heart attack means low risk” (✓ LDL-C and HDL-C dip for up to 2 months after ACS; peri-event values still inform treatment); “Plasma 3% below serum is a lab error” (✓ serum runs about 3% higher than plasma).

cues.text: Trap one: every lipid panel needs a twelve-hour fast. No: nonfasting profiles are routine; fasting is considered when triglycerides are very high.
Trap two: a low LDL cholesterol weeks after a heart attack means low risk. No: lipids dip after the event, and those values still inform treatment.
Trap three: plasma three percent below serum is a laboratory error. No: serum normally runs about three percent higher.

props.title: ✗ “Low LDL-C after a heart attack = low risk.”

scenes.title: Cream on top, cloud below
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “CREAM on top = Chylomicrons; CLOUD below = VLDL; Serum Sits a little higher.” Tokens: cream = chylomicrons · cloud = VLDL · serum ≈ +3%. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: cream on top means chylomicrons, a cloud below means VLDL, and serum sits a little higher than plasma.

Where it breaks: the standing test is only qualitative and cannot measure or genotype anything; it does not identify remnant disease such as type 3; and VLDL clouds the plasma only when triglycerides are high.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Nonfasting is routine · fast if TG very high · tourniquet and standing concentrate”, “Cream = chylomicrons · post-event dip still informative · serum ≈ 3% above plasma”.

cues.text: Lipid profiles can be drawn nonfasting unless triglycerides are very high, a creamy layer on standing plasma means chylomicrons, lipids dip for weeks after a heart attack yet still guide treatment, and serum runs about three percent above plasma.

props.label: Nonfasting routine · fast if TG very high · tourniquet concentrates
Cream = chylomicrons · post-event dip informative · serum ≈ +3%

explanation.what: Plain language: lipid numbers move with meals, how the blood is drawn, which tube is used and what has recently happened to the patient. Most of these effects are small or predictable, so labs now accept nonfasting samples, and a simple overnight tube in the fridge shows whether fat particles from food are still floating in fasting plasma. Scientific terms: nonfasting lipid profile, postprandial change, haemoconcentration, serum–plasma matrix difference, intra-individual biological variation, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), standing (refrigerated) plasma test, supernatant, infranatant, chylomicrons, VLDL, HLP types 1, 4 and 5.
explanation.why: Fasting rarely changes management and makes testing harder to obtain; recognising expected shifts avoids repeat draws, false alarms and false reassurance. Chylomicrons are light enough to float, so a cream layer after a 12–14 h fast marks pathological persistence.
explanation.measure: Nonfasting changes (mean maximum 1–6 h after meals): TG +26 mg/dL; TC and LDL-C −8 mg/dL; HDL-C, apoA1, apoB, Lp(a) unchanged. Consider fasting when nonfasting TG >440 mg/dL (EAS/EFLM) or >400 mg/dL (PSLD/PoLA). Tourniquet ≥3 min or standing >30 min: up to 10–12% rise. Serum about 3% above plasma. After ACS: LDL-C and HDL-C lower, TG higher from 24–96 h, persisting up to 2 months.
explanation.differs: Cream over clear (chylomicrons, type 1) vs cream over turbid (chylomicrons + VLDL, type 5) vs turbid without cream (large VLDL, type 4); expected serum–plasma difference vs analytical error; post-ACS dip vs true low risk.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret a standing plasma tube, decide whether a nonfasting sample is acceptable, explain a serum–plasma gap, or handle a lipid panel drawn soon after a heart attack.

questions.stem: Plasma from a patient who fasted 14 hours is refrigerated overnight. A creamy layer floats on top of a clear infranatant. Which lipoprotein pattern does this indicate?

options.text: Chylomicrons persisting after fasting, as in familial chylomicronaemia (type 1)
options.rationale: Correct. Chylomicrons float as a cream layer; persistence after a 12–14 h fast is pathological, and a clear infranatant means VLDL is not markedly raised.
Incorrect. VLDL excess makes the plasma diffusely turbid without a floating cream layer.
Incorrect. Type 5 gives a cream layer over a turbid, not clear, infranatant.
Incorrect. LDL does not make plasma turbid or form a cream layer.

questions.stem: A lipid panel drawn 3 weeks after an acute coronary syndrome shows a lower LDL-C than the patient’s previous results. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: LDL-C can be lower for up to 2 months after ACS, but the value is still informative and should not be read as low risk
options.rationale: Correct. A 2022 review reports lower LDL-C and HDL-C from 24–96 h after ACS, persisting up to 2 months, and says peri-ACS values are still informative.

options.text: The low LDL-C shows the patient is now at low cardiovascular risk
options.rationale: Incorrect. The dip reflects the acute event, not lower risk.

options.text: The result is invalid and no lipid-based decision may be made for a year
options.rationale: Incorrect. No source supports a year-long wait; peri-event values remain informative.

options.text: Lipids rise after a heart attack, so the true LDL-C is even lower
options.rationale: Incorrect. LDL-C falls, not rises, after ACS; triglycerides tend to rise.

questions.stem: A total cholesterol measured on EDTA plasma is about 3% lower than a serum result drawn at the same time. What is the best explanation?

options.text: An expected serum–plasma difference: serum lipids run about 3% higher than plasma
options.rationale: Correct. The PSLD/PoLA guideline states serum TC, HDL-C, LDL-C and TG are about 3% higher than plasma.

options.text: An analytical error that requires recalibration
options.rationale: Incorrect. A gap of this size and direction is expected between the two matrices.

options.text: Haemoconcentration from a prolonged tourniquet on the plasma draw
options.rationale: Incorrect. Haemoconcentration raises, not lowers, lipid results.
Incorrect. Meals change total cholesterol only slightly, and both tubes were drawn together.

references.usedFor: Same preanalytical statements as the 2024 edition (tourniquet/standing haemoconcentration 10–12%; serum about 3% higher than plasma); confirms stability of the recommendation.

references.citation: Berberich AJ, Hegele RA. A Modern Approach to Dyslipidemia. Endocr Rev. 2022;43(4):611-653. doi:10.1210/endrev/bnab037
references.usedFor: Lower LDL-C and HDL-C and higher TG 24–96 h after ACS, persisting up to 2 months; peri-ACS values still informative; fasting or nonfasting screening, repeat fasting profile if TG >400 mg/dL; chylomicronaemic plasma develops a cream-like supernatant over a clear infranatant on overnight standing.

references.citation: Brahm A, Hegele RA. Hypertriglyceridemia. Nutrients. 2013;5(3):981-1001. doi:10.3390/nu5030981
references.usedFor: HLP type 1: pathological persistence of chylomicrons after a 12–14 h fast; cream-like supernatant above a virtually clear infranatant; HLP type 5: chylomicrons after 12–14 h fasting plus raised VLDL, creamy supernatant with possibly turbid infranatant; HLP type 4: isolated VLDL elevation, serum may appear turbid at the higher end of TG.

claims.text: Nonfasting lipid profiles are routine; mean meal effects; when to consider fasting (TG >440 or >400 mg/dL, before TG-raising drugs, after TG pancreatitis).
Tourniquet ≥3 min or standing >30 min raises lipids 10–12%; serum about 3% above plasma; biological variability; pregnancy TG rise.
After ACS, LDL-C and HDL-C fall and TG rise from 24–96 h, persisting up to 2 months; peri-ACS values remain informative; TC and LDL-C lower for several weeks after a CV event.
Standing plasma test patterns: cream over clear (type 1), cream over turbid (type 5), turbid without cream (type 4 at high TG); chylomicrons persisting after 12–14 h fast are pathological.

Reviewer specifics: 12-hour fast for TG/LDL-C; wait 8 weeks after trauma/infection and 3–4 months postpartum; tourniquet <1–2 min; seated 5 min; chylomicrons clear within 6–9 h; EDTA preferred because it stabilizes the sample.
claims.note: Not taught as facts: no open source read in this session states these figures. The Endotext chapter on infection and lipids (NCBI Bookshelf) returned a reCAPTCHA page. Solnica 2024 accepts serum or plasma and does not state that EDTA is preferred.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 18 Hit 14 requires a 12-hour fast for TG and LDL-C. The EAS/EFLM consensus (Nordestgaard 2016) recommends routine nonfasting lipid profiles, with fasting considered when nonfasting TG >440 mg/dL; the PSLD/PoLA 2024 guideline and Berberich 2022 suggest a repeat fasting profile when TG >400 mg/dL. European/North American sources; Philippine guidelines not covered (register flag rv-lipid-fasting-not-routine).

Ch. 18 Exam Trap 4 says to wait at least 8 weeks before measuring lipoproteins after an acute event, applied to a heart attack. Berberich 2022: LDL-C and HDL-C are lower (TG higher) from 24–96 h after ACS, persisting up to 2 months, but peri-ACS values are still informative and clinicians no longer need to defer treatment decisions (register flag rv-post-acs-lipids-informative).
